paper.title: Gender gaps from labor market shocks
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability (p. 13): "The authors do not have permission to share data." No Statistics Denmark project number, code repository or replication package is mentioned.

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish employer-employee matched register data
registers.role: sample frame; treatment (plant closures); outcomes (unemployment, earnings, changes in earnings); matching covariates

registers.name_in_paper: information on unemployment insurance and social assistance
registers.role: outcomes: constructing the measure of non-participation (exits from the labor market)

registers.name_in_paper: mandatory pension payments / mandatory pension scheme contributions
registers.role: construction of hours worked and of the labor market experience measure
controls, matching covariates and subgroup definitions: sex, education, age, place of residence, marital status and the number of children below 18 in the household; family information in Table 1
variables_mentioned: number of children below the age of 18 in the household

linkages: Workers linked to workplaces and plants through the Danish employer-employee matched register data

Individuals linked to background information on sex, education, age, place of residence, marital status and the number of children below 18 in the household; the number of children is based on residency
Displaced workers linked one-to-one, without replacement, to never-displaced control workers of the same gender by coarsened exact matching on pre-displacement characteristics
Displaced men linked to displaced women through the re-matching regression Eq. (1), producing the 're-matched' sample of men similar to the women
Partners linked to workers for the male income share and the 'age relative to partner' variable in Table 1

sample.universe: Workers in Danish private-sector workplaces with at least five workers in the manufacturing industry, 1995-2006, drawn from register data covering the universe of Danish workplaces and all their workers
selection_rules: Private-sector workplaces with at least five workers; a workplace is classified as closing if its number of workers falls by 90% or more between year t-3 and t
Workplaces where more than 50 percent of the displaced workers remain co-workers the following year are not counted as closing (to exclude mergers and administrative changes in legal structure)

Treatment group: men and women employed at the closing plant within manufacturing at least one year before the first year of closure (they may be displaced in the first, second or third year of the closure)
Only workers with one plant closure between 1995 and 2006; workers treated more than once are excluded (about a 7.5% reduction in person-year observations)
Exclude workers who are students, self-employed, top managers, and those on (part-time) early retirement in the event year; future labor market outcomes are not conditioned on

Control group: workers who never experience a plant closure, with the same set of restrictions as the displaced workers, assigned a random pseudo-event year following the same distribution of years as plant closures

One-to-one coarsened exact matching without replacement, separately for men and women, on t-1 quintiles of earnings, marital status, age, educational groups, quintiles of tenure at the firm, unemployment status, labor market experience and industry (27 code classification)
sample.n_individuals: 133,768 unique individuals, half of them treated due to 1:1 matching; 47,668 treated men and 19,230 treated women, a female share of 30% (Table 1 reports 47,678 men and 19,234 women per group)

construction_notes: Unemployment: the individual is unemployed for at least 12 weeks in year t; in the figure notes, an indicator equal to 1 if the individual is claiming benefits for at least 3 months in a calendar year
Labor earnings: total labor income of the individual in year t; earnings are adjusted for inflation and reported in 2019-levels (Table 1 note)
Changes in earnings: ratio of labor earnings at time t to the average earnings of the individual in the three years prior to the year before the plant closure (t*-4, t*-3 and t*-2)

Labor market participation: the fraction of the year the individual is employed or actively searching; non-participation is the fraction of the year the individual is neither working nor complying with the active labor market policies (neither working nor registered as unemployed)
Labor market experience and hours worked are inferred from mandatory pension payments
Continuous matching variables are discretized before matching (quintiles in the text; the Fig. B1 note says deciles); partner's age and income in t-2 are not matched on
Displaced workers are categorized as treated the year they separate from the closing plant; displacement occurs between event time -1 and 0

Ninety-five percent of the plants close fully and retain zero workers; the remaining 5% retain on average 2.4 workers (median 1). Workers are displaced from plants with on average 185 workers (median 53)
The number of children is based on residency: children not living with the parent are excluded and stepchildren in the household are included
The decomposition covariates in Table 2 are measured in the year prior to displacement, including the age of the youngest child
Attrition is limited to migration out of Denmark and mortality: 80.5% of individuals are observed for all 12 years, 6.2% for 11 years and 1.1% for fewer than 6 years
Eq. (2) is estimated separately for the sample of men and the sample of women, allowing the full set of fixed effects to vary by sex

claims.statement: Job displacement caused by a plant closure changes unemployment for displaced men by 0.0982 in the year of displacement, relative to matched non-displaced workers of the same gender.

treatment.label: PlantClosure: job displacement caused by a plant closure

definition.value: Dummy equal to one in year t+k since the job displacement of worker i. A private-sector workplace with at least five workers is classified as closing if its number of workers falls by 90% or more between year t-3 and t; workers must have at least one year of tenure before the plant closes and must have experienced one plant closure between 1995 and 2006; they are categorized as treated the year they separate from the closing plant. Controls are workers who never experience a plant closure, matched one-to-one (coarsened exact matching, separately by sex) on pre-displacement characteristics.

timing.value: Event year t = the year the worker separates from the closing plant; displacement occurs between event time -1 and 0; closures 1995-2006

definition.value: Indicator for whether individual i is unemployed for at least 12 weeks in year t; in the figure notes: an indicator taking the value 1 if the individual is claiming benefits for at least 3 months in a calendar year

timing.value: Measured in the year of displacement (event time t); effects are estimated for event times -6 to +6 with k = -1 omitted

units.value: probability of being unemployed (coefficients are shares; the text reads them as percentage points)

magnitude.interpretation: The text reads this as an increase in the risk of unemployment of around 9.8 percentage points for men

estimand.target_population: displaced men displaced by a manufacturing plant closure in Denmark, 1995-2006
estimand.time_horizon: year of displacement (event time t); Eq. (2) traces effects from 6 years before to 6 years after the event
estimand.formal_query: E[Y_t(displaced) - Y_t(not displaced) | displaced, event time t = 0]

population.description: displaced men from Danish manufacturing plant closures 1995-2006, together with a one-to-one coarsened-exact-matched control group of never-displaced workers of the same gender
subgroups_defined: men re-matched to resemble the displaced women
education (high school or less, vocational training, higher education)
children below 18 in the household / no children
population.selection: Employed at a manufacturing plant with at least five workers at least one year before the first year of closure, one plant closure between 1995 and 2006; students, self-employed, top managers and workers on (part-time) early retirement in the event year excluded; future labor market outcomes not conditioned on; controls never experience a plant closure and are matched one-to-one on coarsened pre-displacement characteristics separately by sex

identification.source_of_variation: Full plant closures in Danish manufacturing 1995-2006 (a workplace with at least five workers losing 90% or more of its workers between t-3 and t), a firm-level shock that makes the job loss and its timing plausibly exogenous to the individual

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: labor market outcomes of displaced and control workers would have evolved similarly in the absence of the plant closure
key_assumptions.supported_by: Leads to the event: for unemployment and earnings none of the pre-period coefficients are significantly different from zero (Figs. 1-2, Tables L.4-L.7); balancing tests in Appendix B

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: displacement has no effect on outcomes before the event year
key_assumptions.supported_by: Absence of meaningful effects in the pre-period (pre-event coefficients for k < -1)

implies_edges.from: job displacement (plant closure)
implies_edges.to: outcome measured before the event year

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the plant closure does not affect the control group
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix C shows displaced workers are spread across municipalities; the preferred specification includes municipality-specific year fixed effects to absorb local labor market effects

implies_edges.from: job displacement (plant closure) of treated workers

key_assumptions.assumption: Displacement is exogenous to the individual conditional on the matching covariates and the fixed effects: a full plant closure is a firm-level shock, so the timing of job loss is plausibly exogenous to the worker
key_assumptions.supported_by: Plant closures (90% or more of workers displaced) rather than mass layoffs; one-to-one coarsened exact matching on pre-displacement characteristics; balancing tests in Appendix B; absence of pre-trends read as absence of dynamic selectivity

rhs: unobserved worker determinants of future labor market outcomes

implies_edges.from: matched pre-displacement characteristics (earnings quintile, marital status, age, education, tenure quintile, unemployment status, experience, industry)

key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample construction described in Section 2.3; outcomes are not conditioned on

threats_discussed: Anticipation effects / dynamic selectivity into closing plants (checked with pre-event coefficients)
Plant closures large enough to affect the local labor market, which would also hit the control group (footnote 15; municipality x year fixed effects)
Sensitivity to the plant-size cut-off in the closure definition (Appendix E)
Heterogeneity between workers leaving in the first versus the last year of a multi-year closure ('early leavers', Appendix F)
Bias of two-way fixed effects event studies with differential treatment timing (Sun and Abraham, 2021; Goodman-Bacon, 2021 decomposition, Appendix G)
Pre-displacement sorting of men and women across sectors, sub-sectors, firms and plants (Appendices I and J)
robustness_checks: Dropping workers displaced from plants with fewer than 10 workers hardly changes the point estimates (Appendix E)
Only including plants with 50 or more workers reduces the sample by 35%, estimates become less precise and the gender gaps in unemployment and earnings shrink (Appendix E)
Restricting to plants that close within one calendar year, and excluding 'early leavers' (Appendix F)
Sun and Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted estimator: estimates virtually identical to baseline (Appendix G)
Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition: no negative weights (Appendix G)
Adding pre-displacement sector, 6-digit NACE sub-sector and plant fixed effects (Appendix I)
Estimating Eq. (2) in the female-dominated Food, Drinks & Tobacco sub-sector (Appendix K)
Conditioning on non-zero working hours, and alternative outcomes: any employment, hours worked (Appendix D)
unresolved_confounders: Spillovers of large plant closures onto the local labor market, which would also affect the control group (footnote 15: addressed, not ruled out, by municipality x year fixed effects)

fixed_effects: municipality-specific year fixed effects (theta_t x delta_j)

estimation.clustering: standard errors clustered at the individual level

evidence.how: Eq. (2) as printed on page 5 of the PDF, transcribed; the source sets it in Unicode mathematical italics, rendered here as ASCII identifiers (beta_k, theta_t, delta_j).

value.as_printed: Y_{i,j,t} = alpha + sum_{k=-6, t != -1}^{6} beta_k PlantClosure_{i,j,t+k} + sum_{k=-6, t != -1}^{6} lambda_k Time_{i,j,t+k} + theta_t + theta_t x delta_j + u_{i,j,t}

value.claimed_domain: Other countries with different labor markets, and other industries: the authors expect gender gaps following displacement to be larger in other countries, and lower in industries where more workers have formal education and the gender gap in educational attainment is smaller.
boundary_conditions: Gender gaps following lay-offs in other sectors 'likely depend on the gender gaps in human capital'
Denmark combines a flexible labor market, generous parental leave and heavily subsidised child care, which the authors argue makes the gaps they measure a lower bound relative to other contexts
The gender gap in unemployment is said to disappear for workers with formal education (vocational diploma or higher)

We utilize plant closures in Denmark to estimate gender gaps in labor market outcomes and document that women face an increased risk of unemployment and lose a larger share of their earnings in the two years following job displacement.

A private-sector workplace with at least five workers is classified as closing if its number of workers falls by 90% or more between year t-3 and t; workers must have at least one year of tenure before the plant closes and must have experienced one plant closure between 1995 and 2006; they are categorized as treated the year they separate from the closing plant. Controls are workers who never experience a plant closure, matched one-to-one (coarsened exact matching, separately by sex) on pre-displacement characteristics.

timing.value: Event year t = the year the worker separates from the closing plant; displacement occurs between event time -1 and 0; closures 1995-2006

definition.value: Indicator for whether individual i is unemployed for at least 12 weeks in year t; in the figure notes: an indicator taking the value 1 if the individual is claiming benefits for at least 3 months in a calendar year

timing.value: Measured in the year of displacement (event time t); effects are estimated for event times -6 to +6 with k = -1 omitted

units.value: probability of being unemployed (coefficients are shares; the text reads them as percentage points)

estimand.target_population: displaced men re-matched to resemble the displaced women, high school or less, men re-matched to resemble displaced women displaced by a manufacturing plant closure in Denmark, 1995-2006
estimand.time_horizon: year of displacement (event time t); Eq. (2) traces effects from 6 years before to 6 years after the event
estimand.formal_query: E[Y_t(displaced) - Y_t(not displaced) | displaced, event time t = 0]

threats_discussed: Anticipation effects / dynamic selectivity into closing plants (checked with pre-event coefficients)
Plant closures large enough to affect the local labor market, which would also hit the control group (footnote 15; municipality x year fixed effects)
Sensitivity to the plant-size cut-off in the closure definition (Appendix E)
Heterogeneity between workers leaving in the first versus the last year of a multi-year closure ('early leavers', Appendix F)
Bias of two-way fixed effects event studies with differential treatment timing (Sun and Abraham, 2021; Goodman-Bacon, 2021 decomposition, Appendix G)
Pre-displacement sorting of men and women across sectors, sub-sectors, firms and plants (Appendices I and J)
robustness_checks: Dropping workers displaced from plants with fewer than 10 workers hardly changes the point estimates (Appendix E)
Only including plants with 50 or more workers reduces the sample by 35%, estimates become less precise and the gender gaps in unemployment and earnings shrink (Appendix E)
Restricting to plants that close within one calendar year, and excluding 'early leavers' (Appendix F)
Sun and Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted estimator: estimates virtually identical to baseline (Appendix G)
Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition: no negative weights (Appendix G)
Adding pre-displacement sector, 6-digit NACE sub-sector and plant fixed effects (Appendix I)
Estimating Eq. (2) in the female-dominated Food, Drinks & Tobacco sub-sector (Appendix K)
Conditioning on non-zero working hours, and alternative outcomes: any employment, hours worked (Appendix D)
unresolved_confounders: Spillovers of large plant closures onto the local labor market, which would also affect the control group (footnote 15: addressed, not ruled out, by municipality x year fixed effects)

A private-sector workplace with at least five workers is classified as closing if its number of workers falls by 90% or more between year t-3 and t; workers must have at least one year of tenure before the plant closes and must have experienced one plant closure between 1995 and 2006; they are categorized as treated the year they separate from the closing plant. Controls are workers who never experience a plant closure, matched one-to-one (coarsened exact matching, separately by sex) on pre-displacement characteristics.

timing.value: Event year t = the year the worker separates from the closing plant; displacement occurs between event time -1 and 0; closures 1995-2006

definition.value: Indicator for whether individual i is unemployed for at least 12 weeks in year t; in the figure notes: an indicator taking the value 1 if the individual is claiming benefits for at least 3 months in a calendar year

timing.value: Measured in the year of displacement (event time t); effects are estimated for event times -6 to +6 with k = -1 omitted

units.value: probability of being unemployed (coefficients are shares; the text reads them as percentage points)

estimand.target_population: displaced men re-matched to resemble the displaced women, vocational training, men re-matched to resemble displaced women displaced by a manufacturing plant closure in Denmark, 1995-2006
estimand.time_horizon: year of displacement (event time t); Eq. (2) traces effects from 6 years before to 6 years after the event
estimand.formal_query: E[Y_t(displaced) - Y_t(not displaced) | displaced, event time t = 0]

threats_discussed: Anticipation effects / dynamic selectivity into closing plants (checked with pre-event coefficients)
Plant closures large enough to affect the local labor market, which would also hit the control group (footnote 15; municipality x year fixed effects)
Sensitivity to the plant-size cut-off in the closure definition (Appendix E)
Heterogeneity between workers leaving in the first versus the last year of a multi-year closure ('early leavers', Appendix F)
Bias of two-way fixed effects event studies with differential treatment timing (Sun and Abraham, 2021; Goodman-Bacon, 2021 decomposition, Appendix G)
Pre-displacement sorting of men and women across sectors, sub-sectors, firms and plants (Appendices I and J)
robustness_checks: Dropping workers displaced from plants with fewer than 10 workers hardly changes the point estimates (Appendix E)
Only including plants with 50 or more workers reduces the sample by 35%, estimates become less precise and the gender gaps in unemployment and earnings shrink (Appendix E)
Restricting to plants that close within one calendar year, and excluding 'early leavers' (Appendix F)
Sun and Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted estimator: estimates virtually identical to baseline (Appendix G)
Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition: no negative weights (Appendix G)
Adding pre-displacement sector, 6-digit NACE sub-sector and plant fixed effects (Appendix I)
Estimating Eq. (2) in the female-dominated Food, Drinks & Tobacco sub-sector (Appendix K)
Conditioning on non-zero working hours, and alternative outcomes: any employment, hours worked (Appendix D)

A private-sector workplace with at least five workers is classified as closing if its number of workers falls by 90% or more between year t-3 and t; workers must have at least one year of tenure before the plant closes and must have experienced one plant closure between 1995 and 2006; they are categorized as treated the year they separate from the closing plant. Controls are workers who never experience a plant closure, matched one-to-one (coarsened exact matching, separately by sex) on pre-displacement characteristics.

timing.value: Event year t = the year the worker separates from the closing plant; displacement occurs between event time -1 and 0; closures 1995-2006

definition.value: Indicator for whether individual i is unemployed for at least 12 weeks in year t; in the figure notes: an indicator taking the value 1 if the individual is claiming benefits for at least 3 months in a calendar year

timing.value: Measured in the year of displacement (event time t); effects are estimated for event times -6 to +6 with k = -1 omitted

units.value: probability of being unemployed (coefficients are shares; the text reads them as percentage points)

estimand.target_population: displaced men re-matched to resemble the displaced women, higher education, men re-matched to resemble displaced women displaced by a manufacturing plant closure in Denmark, 1995-2006
estimand.time_horizon: year of displacement (event time t); Eq. (2) traces effects from 6 years before to 6 years after the event
estimand.formal_query: E[Y_t(displaced) - Y_t(not displaced) | displaced, event time t = 0]

population.description: displaced men re-matched to resemble the displaced women, higher education, men re-matched to resemble displaced women from Danish manufacturing plant closures 1995-2006, together with a one-to-one coarsened-exact-matched control group of never-displaced workers of the same gender
subgroups_defined: men re-matched to resemble the displaced women
education (high school or less, vocational training, higher education)
children below 18 in the household / no children
population.selection: Employed at a manufacturing plant with at least five workers at least one year before the first year of closure, one plant closure between 1995 and 2006; students, self-employed, top managers and workers on (part-time) early retirement in the event year excluded; future labor market outcomes not conditioned on; controls never experience a plant closure and are matched one-to-one on coarsened pre-displacement characteristics separately by sex

identification.source_of_variation: Full plant closures in Danish manufacturing 1995-2006 (a workplace with at least five workers losing 90% or more of its workers between t-3 and t), a firm-level shock that makes the job loss and its timing plausibly exogenous to the individual

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: labor market outcomes of displaced and control workers would have evolved similarly in the absence of the plant closure
key_assumptions.supported_by: Leads to the event: for unemployment and earnings none of the pre-period coefficients are significantly different from zero (Figs. 1-2, Tables L.4-L.7); balancing tests in Appendix B

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: displacement has no effect on outcomes before the event year
key_assumptions.supported_by: Absence of meaningful effects in the pre-period (pre-event coefficients for k < -1)

threats_discussed: Anticipation effects / dynamic selectivity into closing plants (checked with pre-event coefficients)
Plant closures large enough to affect the local labor market, which would also hit the control group (footnote 15; municipality x year fixed effects)
Sensitivity to the plant-size cut-off in the closure definition (Appendix E)
Heterogeneity between workers leaving in the first versus the last year of a multi-year closure ('early leavers', Appendix F)
Bias of two-way fixed effects event studies with differential treatment timing (Sun and Abraham, 2021; Goodman-Bacon, 2021 decomposition, Appendix G)
Pre-displacement sorting of men and women across sectors, sub-sectors, firms and plants (Appendices I and J)
robustness_checks: Dropping workers displaced from plants with fewer than 10 workers hardly changes the point estimates (Appendix E)
Only including plants with 50 or more workers reduces the sample by 35%, estimates become less precise and the gender gaps in unemployment and earnings shrink (Appendix E)
Restricting to plants that close within one calendar year, and excluding 'early leavers' (Appendix F)
Sun and Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted estimator: estimates virtually identical to baseline (Appendix G)
Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition: no negative weights (Appendix G)
Adding pre-displacement sector, 6-digit NACE sub-sector and plant fixed effects (Appendix I)
Estimating Eq. (2) in the female-dominated Food, Drinks & Tobacco sub-sector (Appendix K)
Conditioning on non-zero working hours, and alternative outcomes: any employment, hours worked (Appendix D)
unresolved_confounders: Spillovers of large plant closures onto the local labor market, which would also affect the control group (footnote 15: addressed, not ruled out, by municipality x year fixed effects)

claims.statement: The displacement effect on non-participation does not differ between women and men: both face a 9 percentage point increase in the likelihood of being registered as non-participating.

treatment.label: PlantClosure: job displacement caused by a plant closure

definition.value: Dummy equal to one in year t+k since the job displacement of worker i. A private-sector workplace with at least five workers is classified as closing if its number of workers falls by 90% or more between year t-3 and t; workers must have at least one year of tenure before the plant closes and must have experienced one plant closure between 1995 and 2006; they are categorized as treated the year they separate from the closing plant. Controls are workers who never experience a plant closure, matched one-to-one (coarsened exact matching, separately by sex) on pre-displacement characteristics.

timing.value: Event year t = the year the worker separates from the closing plant; displacement occurs between event time -1 and 0; closures 1995-2006

treatment.label: PlantClosure: job displacement caused by a plant closure

definition.value: Dummy equal to one in year t+k since the job displacement of worker i. Restricting to plants that close within one calendar year, and excluding 'early leavers' (Appendix F)
Sun and Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted estimator: estimates virtually identical to baseline (Appendix G)
Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition: no negative weights (Appendix G)
Adding pre-displacement sector, 6-digit NACE sub-sector and plant fixed effects (Appendix I)
Estimating Eq. (2) in the female-dominated Food, Drinks & Tobacco sub-sector (Appendix K)
Conditioning on non-zero working hours, and alternative outcomes: any employment, hours worked (Appendix D)
unresolved_confounders: Spillovers of large plant closures onto the local labor market, which would also affect the control group (footnote 15)

evidence.annotation: Fig. K1. Notes: Job displacement between -1 and 0. Black triangles denote displaced men, while green circles denote displaced women, relative to an equal size control group of workers of their own gender who are not displaced.

value.as_printed: Y_{i,j,t} = alpha + sum_{k=-6, t != -1}^{6} beta_k PlantClosure_{i,j,t+k} + sum_{k=-6, t != -1}^{6} lambda_k Time_{i,j,t+k} + theta_t + theta_t x delta_j + u_{i,j,t}
value.normalisation: Event time k = -1 (the year before displacement) is omitted from both summations, so all PlantClosure and Time coefficients are relative to the year before displacement; Eq. (2) is estimated separately for men and women with the full set of fixed effects allowed to vary by sex.

value.claimed_domain: Other countries with different labor markets, and other industries: the authors expect gender gaps following displacement to be larger in other countries, and lower in industries where more workers have formal education and the gender gap in educational attainment is smaller.
boundary_conditions: Gender gaps following lay-offs in other sectors 'likely depend on the gender gaps in human capital'
Denmark combines a flexible labor market, generous parental leave and heavily subsidised child care, which the authors argue makes the gaps they measure a lower bound relative to other contexts
The gender gap in unemployment is said to disappear for workers with formal education (vocational diploma or higher)
